questions.question: What extra structure makes $\mathbb{R}^n$ a Euclidean space rather than just a coordinate vector space?
options: The standard basis, giving every vector unique coordinates
Componentwise addition and scaling of real $n$-tuples
The determinant, giving signed volumes spanned by $n$ vectors
The standard inner product, giving lengths and angles

questions.question: Why does it make sense to speak about angles between vectors in Euclidean space?
options: Because the standard inner product gives the cosine formula
Because coordinate axes alone fix angles, with no product needed
Because the determinant of the two vectors gives their angle
Because the lengths $\|x\|$ and $\|y\|$ alone determine the angle

questions.question: What is the Euclidean distance between $(1,2)$ and $(4,6)$?
options: $\sqrt{7}$

questions.question: Why does the word “standard” matter in the standard inner product on $\mathbb{R}^n$?
options: It signals that $\mathbb{R}^n$ admits only one inner product
It means $x\cdot y$ equals the product of lengths $\|x\|\|y\|$
It picks out the dot product and so the usual geometry
It means the inner product of two vectors is always $0$ or $1$

questions.question: Why is $\mathbb{C}^n$ not the coordinate space used to define Euclidean space?
options: Because Euclidean space is a real space with the dot product
Because $\mathbb{C}^n$ is not closed under vector addition and scaling
Because $\mathbb{C}^n$ admits no inner product of any kind
Because $\mathbb{C}^n$ has no basis, so its vectors have no coordinates

questions.question: Equip $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the inner product $\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle=2x_1y_1+x_2y_2$. In this Euclidean space, what is the length $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|=\sqrt{\langle\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{v}\rangle}$ of $\boldsymbol{v}=(1,1)$?
options: $\sqrt{3}$
$\sqrt{2}$
$\sqrt{5}$

questions.question: A Euclidean space is a finite-dimensional real vector space with an inner product. Write real polynomials as $p(x)=\sum_k a_kx^k$ and $q(x)=\sum_k b_kx^k$ with finitely many nonzero coefficients, and let $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})$ be the space of real polynomials of degree at most $2$. Which of these pairs is a Euclidean space?
options: $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})$ with $\langle p,q\rangle=a_0b_0+a_1b_1+a_2b_2$
$\mathbb{R}^2$ with $\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle=x_1y_1-x_2y_2$
$\mathbb{R}^2$ with $\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle=|x_1y_1|+|x_2y_2|$
All real polynomials, of any degree, with $\langle p,q\rangle=\sum_k a_kb_k$

questions.question: Equip $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle=2x_1y_1+x_2y_2$. A basis is orthonormal when its vectors are mutually orthogonal and have length $1$ for this inner product. Which list is an orthonormal basis of this Euclidean space?
options: $\bigl(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(1,1),\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(1,-1)\bigr)$
